newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: CONFRAM , ROMATEX UP ON PLANNED LINK.
newsitem.headline: CONFRAM , ROMATEX UP ON PLANNED LINK.

text.p: Shares in Romatex Ltd, the South African clothing and textile company which is in takeover talks with Consolidated Frame Textiles Ltd (Confram), surged 33 percent on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange (JSE) on Tuesday.
Mike Hankinson, managing director of Romatex, confirmed that talks with Confram on taking a controlling stake in his company were taking place.
"Talks are at an advanced stage...(and we expect a deal) rather sooner than later," he told Reuters on Tuesday.
He said the Competition Board would have to approve the deal, but he did not foresee any problems obtaining the watchdog body's approval.

He declined to comment on the pricing of the proposed deal but analysts said there was talk of a price tag of 56 million rand to be paid to Romatex parent C.G. Smith Ltd which holds a 60 percent stake.
A further 20 percent could be bought from Associated Furniture Companies Ltd , they said.

C.G. Smith Ltd said on Monday it was engaged in discussions regarding its stake in Romatex. At the same time, Confram also said it was in talks which could have an impact on its share price and that of parent Frame Group Holdings Ltd .
Dealers and analysts said on Tuesday the market had welcomed news that that Confram, the country's largest textile firm may take up to an 80 percent stake in Romatex.
"It is the most positive thing we have heard from the sector in a long time," said Campbell Parry, analyst at Simpson McKie James Capel.

By 1300 GMT, shares in Romatex were up 125 cents to five rand after 137,000 shares had changed hands. Romatex shares touched a year low of three rand on August 20. Confram shares added 30 cents, or almost six percent, to 550 cents.

Another analyst who asked not to be identified said: "Both companies can now save on overheads and on manufacturing plants. And with the flood of cheap imports, it is better to be a stronger player with more leverage in the market."

Clothing and textile companies have been hard hit in the past few years by a flood of illegal imports. A further blow was a week long wage strike in July which cost both employers and workers millions of rands in lost wages and production.
